subject: botany_2
question_text: How does ascent of sap occur in tall trees?

mark_split.label: Why it works in tall trees

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.21, printed question 9. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Revised 2026-09-05 after the examiner audit: the insider note's mark arithmetic was corrected against this card's own mark split, the s2 heading line no longer counts transpiration pull as a physical property of water, and the s3 memory tip no longer denies that root pressure pushes from below.

insider_note: Three names carry two of the four marks: cohesion and adhesion share one mark, transpiration pull has its own. Name all three even if you explain only briefly — a missing name cannot be recovered by a longer sentence about the others.

steps.label: Ascent of sap defined
steps.margin_note: Definition, tissue, and the direction. Three or four lines.
lines: Ascent of sap is the upward movement of water
from the roots to the leaves.
It moves through the XYLEM.
It moves against the force of gravity.
steps.why: Naming the tissue and the direction fixes what has to be explained: an upward flow with no pump, which is why the rest of the answer is about physical properties of water.
common_mistakes: Writing phloem. Water rises through the XYLEM; phloem carries food.
Leaving out 'against gravity'. That is the difficulty the answer has to explain.
steps.memory_tip: Sap goes up the xylem; food goes down the phloem.

steps.label: Cohesion and adhesion
steps.margin_note: Both names, both meanings, one line each. Do not merge them into one sentence.
lines: The ascent depends on two physical properties
of water and one driving force.
1. Cohesion: the mutual attraction between
water molecules. It holds the water column
together as one unbroken thread.
2. Adhesion: the attraction of water molecules
to polar surfaces, such as the walls of the
tracheal elements.
steps.why: Cohesion holds the column together and adhesion holds it against the wall, so between them the water in a tall xylem vessel behaves like a single rope rather than loose drops.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two. COHESION is water to water; ADHESION is water to the wall.
Defining only one. The mark asks for both names with their meanings.
steps.memory_tip: Cohesion is water holding water; adhesion is water holding the wall.

steps.label: Transpiration pull
steps.margin_note: Evaporation, tension, pull. Name it as the driving force in the last line.
lines: 3. Transpiration pull:
Water evaporates from the leaf surface during
transpiration.
This creates a tension at the top of the water
column.
The tension pulls the whole column upward.
Transpiration pull is the driving force for the
upward movement of water.
steps.why: Transpiration is what actually supplies the force; cohesion and adhesion only make it possible for that force to be felt all the way down to the root.
common_mistakes: Calling it a push from the roots. Root pressure is small; the main force is a PULL from the top.
Leaving out evaporation. The pull begins when water leaves the leaf.
steps.memory_tip: Evaporation at the leaf pulls the column up; root pressure is too small to lift water in a tall tree.

steps.label: Why it works in tall trees
steps.margin_note: Close on tensile strength and capillarity. This is the mark for the word 'tall'.

lines.text: High tensile strength plus high capillarity

lines: Together these properties give water a high
tensile strength and high capillarity.
So the water column does not break even in a
very tall tree.
Photosynthesis needs a steady water supply,
and the xylem from root to leaf delivers it.
steps.why: The question says TALL trees, so the answer has to close on the reason height is not a problem: the column has enough tensile strength to hold together over that distance.
common_mistakes: Not answering the 'tall' part. The last mark is for why the column does not break.
Writing that a pump lifts the water. There is no pump in a plant.
steps.memory_tip: An unbroken rope of water can be pulled from the top however long it is.
